title: Geospatial Computing
text:
Modul: Geospatial Computing
Modulleitung: Nils Ratnaweera
Essential Information
By focusing on computational approaches to working with geospatial data, you will continue and deepen your understanding of classical GIS workflows.
You will primarily use R as the scripting environment, drawing on your existing programming experience. Script-based workflows are complemented by graphical GIS tools, e.g. desktop GIS software, to support the exploration, analysis, and visualization of spatial data. In addition, you are introduced to the use of AI and large language models (LLMs) as supporting tools for geospatial problem-solving, coding, and analytical reasoning.
Through emphasizing applied, problem-oriented learning, you will be prepared to handle complex geospatial tasks in environmental and spatial analysis contexts.
Module Contents

Advanced concepts of vector and raster geospatial data
Script-based spatial data processing and analysis
Integration of scripting workflows with GUI-based GIS tools
Spatial analysis and transformation of geospatial datasets
Visualization and communication of spatial information
Automation and reproducibility of geospatial workflows
AI-assisted approaches to geospatial analysis and coding
Applied case studies in environmental and spatial data analysis

title: Geospatial Computing — Course Planning Meeting
text:
Proposed Course Framework
The course is organised along two axes: methods and domains.

Methods Axis
Each lecturer teaches one or more method blocks. Each block is anchored to a specific application domain (see below), giving students a concrete dataset and problem to work with. The following methods are currently on the list — part of the meeting agenda is to reduce / enhance and confirm this list:

Spatial pattern analysis — autocorrelation, hotspot analysis, interpolation
Uncertainty quantification — Monte Carlo simulation, error propagation, sensitivity analysis
Image processing — automated detection from camera trap imagery (e.g. MegaDetector)
Multi-Criteria Analysis (MCA) — spatial suitability modelling, decision support
Network Analysis — routing, connectivity, accessibility


We likely have capacity for 3–4 of these, not all five. Selection is a key agenda item.



Domains Axis
Each method block is taught in the context of one application domain. Students then choose a domain for their own semester project and apply the methods they have learned. Current candidate domains:

Wildlife Monitoring — camera trap data, opportunistic species observations
Vegetation Ecology — spatial and temporal vegetation surveys
Hydrology — vectorised river networks (no remote sensing or drone data)
Environmental Planning — visitor management, quiet area mapping



Toolsets
The following tools are introduced where relevant, rather than as standalone blocks:

R / RStudio
QGIS
QGIS Model designer
Building a QGIS Plugin — Python-based extension
Databases (PostGIS / SQLite)
QField
Webmapping

title: Geospatial Computing — Course Concept
text:
Course Structure
The course runs over 14 weeks and is organised around three thematic blocks, each pairing a method focus with an application domain. Each block has a main two-week session and one advanced follow-up session in weeks 9–11. The second half closes with a semester project phase.




Table 1: Weekly Schedule










Topic
Theory
Seminar
Labs




Introduction (rata)​


1
Module Introduction.
course overview & structure, what is geospatial computing, CRS & projections recap

toolchain setup (R, QGIS, RStudio/Positron), first test script


Terrain & Water (murj)​​


2
Raster Data Fundamentals
Recap on raster data model. Dive into spatial resolution, map algebra, MCA

loading rasters in R/QGIS, basic raster operations


3
Terrain Analysis & Hydrological Modelling
DEM sources & quality, terrain derivatives (hillshade/slope/aspect), D8 flow direction algorithm, watershed concepts

terrain function workflow, watershed delineation in QGIS/R


Spatial Ecology & Occurrence (rahn)​​​


4
From Observations to Spatial Data
point data structure, data sources (GBIF, iNaturalist, camera traps), coordinate uncertainty, sampling bias

accessing GBIF via API in R, mapping and filtering occurrence data


5
Spatial Patterns in Point Data
KDE (bandwidth, kernel function), IDW (power parameter, distance decay)

computing KDE & IDW in R/QGIS, comparing outputs with different parameters


Paths & Flows (rata)​​​​


6
Networks & Graph Theory
graph theory basics (nodes, edges, directed/undirected), centrality measures

loading OSM network data, computing centrality with sfnetworks in R


7
Routing & Accessibility Analysis
Dijkstra's algorithm, isochrone concepts, accessibility measures
Implementing Dijkstra «by hand»
computing shortest paths & isochrones in R

10
Webmapping in the Opensource Ecosystem
what is web mapping, server vs. client-side, web-friendly formats, performance challenges with large datasets

converting data to GeoJSON, publishing a webmap (QGIS Cloud or equivalent)

Uncertainty in Geodata
types of uncertainty (positional, attribute, completeness), error propagation, Monte Carlo basics
monte carlo to calculate Pi
routing sensitivity analysis — vary edge weights, compare isochrone results

title: Geospatial Computing — Course Concept
text:
Semester Project
Students carry out a semester-long project in which they apply the methods from all three blocks to a dataset of their choice. The project runs in parallel with the teaching blocks and culminates in a written report.
The oral exam tests understanding of the methods and results — not the project output itself. This guards against unreflective use of AI tools.
